units.title: Unit 71 — Suffixes: forming nouns
units.source: Vocabulary study targets from published reference material; Unit 71. Page information, if available, is retained in sourceAudit.
learningObjectives: Recognise noun forms derived from verbs using -ion, -ation and -ment.
Form abstract nouns from adjectives using -ness and -ity, including spelling changes.
Identify people and occupations through -er, -or and -ist endings.
Recognise shifts in word stress when a suffix changes a word family.
Apply the forms in the unit exercises, including hesitation, arrangement, sadness and activity.

items.example: Our team hopes to invent a cheaper way to save energy.
items.note: Verb; the corresponding noun is invention. Its main stress is on the second syllable.

items.example: The engineer presented her latest invention at the exhibition.
items.note: Noun formed from invent with -ion; both words have stress on the second syllable.

items.example: We need to discuss the project with our neighbours.
items.note: Verb; discuss something, not discuss about something.

items.example: We had a useful discussion about the new timetable.
items.note: Noun from discuss; a discussion about something. The main stress remains on the second syllable.

items.example: Could you translate this email into English?
items.note: Verb; translate something into another language.

items.example: The English translation of the article is now available.
items.note: Noun from translate; a translation of a text into another language.

items.example: I usually relax by walking in the evening.
items.note: Verb; compare the stress with relaxation.

items.example: Music and quiet surroundings can help with relaxation.
items.note: Noun from relax with -ation; the main stress moves to -sa- in relaxation.

items.example: The school is trying to improve its library.
items.note: Verb; an improvement is a positive change.

items.example: There has been a clear improvement in her pronunciation.
items.note: Noun formed with -ment; an improvement in something.

items.example: Elected leaders govern the country for a limited period.
items.note: Verb; the related noun government refers to the body that governs.

items.example: The government announced new plans for public transport.
items.note: Noun formed from govern with -ment; refers to those who govern a country.

items.example: She manages a small restaurant near the station.
items.note: Verb; management is the activity or group responsible for managing.

items.example: Good management can make a small business successful.
items.note: Noun formed from manage with -ment; the final e is removed.

items.example: The company plans to develop a new product next year.
items.note: Verb; development is the corresponding noun.

items.example: The development of the new software took six months.
items.note: Noun from develop with -ment; the stress stays on the second syllable.

items.example: Do not hesitate to ask for help if you need it.
items.note: Verb introduced in the practice table; compare the changed stress in hesitation.

items.example: After a moment of hesitation, she accepted the offer.
items.note: Noun from hesitate with -ation; the primary stress moves towards the end.

items.example: We will arrange a meeting for Thursday afternoon.
items.note: Verb introduced in the practice table; the noun is arrangement.

items.example: The travel arrangements have already been made.
items.note: Noun formed from arrange with -ment; common in the plural for practical plans.

items.example: My legs felt weak after the long walk.
items.note: Adjective; noun: weakness.

items.example: His main weakness is speaking too quickly.
items.note: Noun from weak with -ness; may refer to physical weakness or a weak point.

items.example: She feels happy in her new job.
items.note: Adjective; change final y to i in happiness.

items.example: Spending time with family brings him happiness.
items.note: Noun formed from happy with -ness; the spelling changes y to i.

items.example: He was too ill to go to work yesterday.
items.note: Adjective; common British English word for being unwell.

items.example: She stayed home because of a serious illness.
items.note: Noun from ill with -ness; an illness can be mild or serious.

items.example: Swimming twice a week helps him stay fit.
items.note: Adjective describing good physical condition; noun: fitness.

items.example: Regular exercise can improve your fitness.
items.note: Noun formed from fit with -ness; do not write a double t.

items.example: It was a stupid mistake, but we can correct it.
items.note: Adjective; the noun stupidity has a different main stress.

items.example: He regretted the stupidity of his decision.
items.note: Noun formed using -ity; main stress moves from STU- to -PID-.

items.example: This café is very popular with students.
items.note: Adjective; use popular with a group of people.

items.example: The new sport is growing in popularity.
items.note: Noun formed from popular using -ity; primary stress falls on -LAR-.

items.example: The two designs look very similar.
items.note: Adjective; similar to something, not similar with something.

items.example: There is a clear similarity between the two paintings.
items.note: Noun derived from similar using -ity; a similarity between A and B.

items.example: After training, she was able to swim a kilometre.
items.note: Adjective; be able to do something.

items.example: The role requires the ability to work under pressure.
items.note: Noun formed from able with -ity; ability to do something.

items.example: His inability to hear clearly made the conversation difficult.
items.note: The negative noun form of ability; inability to do something.

items.example: She felt sad when the holiday ended.
items.note: Adjective introduced by the exercise; the noun is sadness.

items.example: There was a feeling of sadness after the goodbye.
items.note: Noun formed from sad with -ness; keep only one d.

items.example: My grandfather is still very active at eighty.
items.note: Adjective introduced in the exercise; corresponding noun: activity.

items.example: Walking is a healthy outdoor activity.
items.note: Noun formed from active using -ity; the main stress changes.

items.pt: bailarino de balé; bailarina de balé
items.example: The ballet dancer practises every morning.
items.note: Person who dances in a ballet; dancer has the agent suffix -er.

items.pt: cantor de música pop; cantora de música pop
items.example: The pop singer released a new album in June.
items.note: Person who sings pop music; singer is formed from sing with -er.

items.pt: jogador profissional de futebol; jogadora profissional de futebol
items.example: Her ambition is to become a professional footballer.
items.note: Footballer is a person who plays football; British English -er job noun.

items.pt: diretor de empresa; diretora de empresa
items.example: The company director approved the new budget.
items.note: A senior person responsible for leading a company; director ends in -or.

items.example: A translator helped us understand the document.
items.note: Person who translates writing; noun formed from translate with -or.

items.pt: ator de cinema; atriz de cinema
items.example: The film actor spoke about his latest role.
items.note: Actor is a person who performs in films or plays; ends in -or.

items.example: The artist paints portraits of local people.
items.note: A person who creates art; an artist can draw, paint or work in other forms.

items.example: An economist explained why food prices were rising.
items.note: A person who studies economics; the stress changes from economics to economist.

items.example: The scientist is researching new materials.
items.note: A person who works in science; ends in -ist.

sectionsChecked: A: Verb + noun suffix: -ion/-ation and -ment; teaching table and sentences
B: Adjective + noun suffix: -ness and -ity; teaching table and sentences
C: -er, -or and -ist for people and jobs; language-help stress box

units.title: Unit 72 — Suffixes: forming adjectives
units.source: Vocabulary study targets from published reference material; Unit 72. Page information, if available, is retained in sourceAudit.
learningObjectives: Recognise and use common adjective endings including -al, -able, -y, -ous and -ive.
Select -able adjectives and their un- opposites according to meaning and context.
Distinguish -ful and -less adjectives and avoid invalid or incorrectly spelled forms.
Describe people, objects, events and opinions with the adjectives studied.
Apply the spelling and derivation patterns to exercise-only examples such as windy, dangerous, creative, emotional and foggy.

items.example: She has always wanted to learn a musical instrument.
items.note: Adjective formed from music using -al; often means related to music.

items.example: They had a political debate at the university.
items.note: Adjective related to politics; a political question or issue.

items.example: An electrical fault stopped the lift from working.
items.note: Often describes systems, equipment or problems involving electricity; compare electric for powered objects.

items.example: That is my personal opinion, not the view of the whole team.
items.note: From person; refers to an individual or something belonging to a person.

items.example: The town holds an annual music festival in July.
items.note: A yearly event; usually one that happens every year.

items.example: The first of January is a national holiday in many countries.
items.note: From nation; belonging or relating to a whole country.

items.example: The museum offers cultural activities for children.
items.note: From culture; related to the beliefs, arts and practices of a society.

items.example: The ceremony has cultural significance for local families.
items.note: In the source text, the phrase describes the importance of numbers in a culture.

items.example: They wore traditional clothes at the celebration.
items.note: From tradition; describes customs or styles passed from one generation to another.

items.example: It is normal to feel nervous before a big exam.
items.note: Usual or expected in a given situation; used in the cultural text.

items.example: We had an enjoyable afternoon by the lake.
items.note: From enjoy with -able; something you enjoy.

items.example: These seats are comfortable on long journeys.
items.note: From comfort with -able; opposite: uncomfortable.

items.example: I felt uncomfortable sitting on the hard bench.
items.note: Opposite of comfortable; it can refer to physical discomfort or a social situation.

items.example: This jacket is suitable for a formal meeting.
items.note: Suitable for a purpose or occasion; opposite: unsuitable.

items.example: Those shoes are unsuitable for a long walk.
items.note: Opposite of suitable; commonly followed by for.

items.example: We need a reliable internet connection for the call.
items.note: Can be trusted or depended on; a reliable person, source or service.

items.example: The old bus service is slow and unreliable.
items.note: Opposite of reliable; note the negative prefix un-.

items.example: She bought a fashionable coat for the winter.
items.note: Describes something currently popular in fashion.

items.example: That style of hat is considered unfashionable now.
items.note: Opposite of fashionable; formed with the prefix un-.

items.example: The shop offered a reasonable price for the repair.
items.note: Fair or sensible in the circumstances; opposite: unreasonable.

items.example: It would be unreasonable to expect the job to finish in an hour.
items.note: Opposite of reasonable; describes demands, expectations or behaviour.

items.example: My sister is sociable and makes friends easily.
items.note: A sociable person enjoys being with other people.

items.example: He is not unfriendly; he is simply a little unsociable.
items.note: Opposite of sociable; not necessarily rude or unfriendly.

items.example: We had an unforgettable trip through the mountains.
items.note: An adjective used more often than forgettable for a memorable experience; double t.

items.example: She told us an unbelievable story about her journey.
items.note: Something surprising or very hard to believe; spelled believe + able, with the final e removed.

items.example: The children decorated the classroom with colourful pictures.
items.note: From colour with -ful; British spelling uses colour. The suffix is -ful, not -full.

items.example: The receptionist was very helpful when we arrived.
items.note: From help with -ful; can describe people, information or actions.

items.example: We stayed in a peaceful village beside a river.
items.note: From peace with -ful; quiet, calm or free from conflict.

items.example: This guide contains useful advice for new students.
items.note: From use with -ful; opposite: useless. Write useful, never usefull.

items.example: This broken charger is useless now.
items.note: From use with -less; the opposite of useful.

items.example: It was painful to walk after I hurt my ankle.
items.note: From pain with -ful; opposite: painless.

items.example: The nurse promised the test would be quick and painless.
items.note: From pain with -less; having or causing no pain.

items.example: Be careful when you cross the busy road.
items.note: From care with -ful; opposite: careless. Spell careful, not carefull.

items.example: A careless mistake changed the final result.
items.note: From care with -less; lacking sufficient attention.

items.example: They chose an attractive design for the new website.
items.note: Exercise-introduced adjective formed from attract with -ive.

items.example: It was cloudy in the morning but sunny later.
items.note: Exercise-introduced adjective formed from cloud with -y.

items.example: The town is famous for its old stone bridge.
items.note: Exercise-introduced adjective from fame with -ous.

items.example: It was too windy to eat outside.
items.note: Exercise-introduced adjective formed from wind with -y.

items.example: It is dangerous to swim here after heavy rain.
items.note: Exercise-introduced adjective formed from danger with -ous.

items.example: The class came up with several creative solutions.
items.note: Exercise-introduced adjective formed from create with -ive.

items.example: The film had a very emotional ending.
items.note: Exercise-introduced adjective from emotion with -al.

items.example: The road was foggy early in the morning.
items.note: Exercise-introduced adjective from fog with -y; double the final g.

items.example: We had a wonderful holiday in the countryside.
items.note: Exercise contrast: -ful does not always have a standard -less opposite; wonderless is not normal English.

items.example: That is a beautiful painting of the coast.
items.note: Exercise contrast: there is no regular everyday adjective beautiless as an opposite of beautiful.

sectionsChecked: A: -al adjectives; Shichi-Go-San cultural text, image and definition callouts
B: -able adjectives and un- opposites; example phrases and definitions
Exercises 72.1–72.6; answer key on PDF page 236
